passage:
Week one: Abhinav bought chips and a fizzy drink every day from the canteen. By football practice he felt heavy and slow, and he kept stopping to catch his breath.
Week two: Mehak, his mother, packed him roti rolls with paneer and a banana. He grumbled. "Try it for a week," she said.
Week three: Abhinav noticed he could run the whole practice without stopping. He still had chips on Fridays, but on other days he ate his tiffin first. "Maybe it's the banana," he joked.

qa.q: What did Mehak pack for Abhinav in week two?
qa.a: She packed him roti rolls with paneer and a banana.

qa.q: What does Abhinav grumbling in week two suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he didn't want to give up his usual snacks and was unsure the change would help.

qa.q: What could Abhinav do to keep the new habit going?
qa.a: He could keep eating his tiffin first and save chips for an occasional treat, as he does on Fridays.

qa.q: How might Abhinav's coach see the change?
qa.a: The coach may notice he has more energy and can play the whole practice.

grounding: It shows a child linking food choices to his energy over several weeks.

passage: "Aparna, in my village when I was your age, we ate ragi rotis, dal, vegetables from the field, and buttermilk. Sweets only on festivals. We walked to school and worked in the fields after. I was never tired. When I came to the city, I started eating fried snacks every day. Soon I felt sleepy after lunch and my stomach grumbled all the time. So I went back to simple food most days and kept the snacks for special occasions." Kishore Thatha put a bowl of fruit in front of her. "Your body is growing. Give it good fuel."

qa.q: What did Kishore eat in his village as a child?
qa.a: He ate ragi rotis, dal, vegetables from the field, and buttermilk.

qa.q: What does Kishore feeling sleepy after lunch in the city suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he noticed that fried snacks every day made him feel worse.

qa.q: What advice does Kishore give Aparna?
qa.a: He tells her to eat simple, good food most days because her body is growing, and keep snacks special.

qa.q: How might Aparna see her own snacks after this story?
qa.a: She may start to think about how her food affects her energy and growth.

grounding: An elder tells a story linking food choices to energy, growth and health.

passage: On the school hiking trip, the snack stall at the base of the hill was the last shop before the long climb. Kashish and her brother Lalit had only enough money for one thing each. Lalit grabbed a cold fizzy drink. Kashish hesitated between the drink and a bunch of bananas with a packet of peanuts. She remembered her teacher saying sugary drinks give quick energy that doesn't last. She chose the bananas and peanuts. Halfway up the hill, Lalit was dragging his feet. Kashish shared a banana. "Okay," Lalit panted, "next time I'm copying you."

qa.q: What did Lalit buy at the snack stall?
qa.a: He grabbed a cold fizzy drink.

qa.q: What was Kashish thinking when she hesitated?
qa.a: She was remembering her teacher's point that sugary drinks give quick energy that doesn't last.

qa.q: Which choice worked better for the climb, and why?
qa.a: Bananas and peanuts, because they gave steadier energy while Lalit tired halfway up.

qa.q: How might Lalit see food choices after the hike?
qa.a: He seems to realise Kashish chose better and says he'll copy her next time.

grounding: It shows a child linking food choices to energy on a hike with little money.

passage: Farhan's cricket match in the Lucknow colony ground was at four. At lunch he skipped Ammi's rajma and rice and ate two packets of chips and a fizzy drink from the corner shop. By the second over he felt heavy and yawny, and he dropped an easy catch. His friend Naveen was running between the wickets like a rocket. 'What did you eat?' Farhan panted at the drinks break. 'Roti, dal, a banana,' Naveen said. 'Same as always.' Farhan's tummy grumbled even though he'd eaten plenty. That night he ate the rajma, twice. Next Saturday, before the match, he asked Ammi for a banana too. He didn't drop anything.

qa.q: What did Farhan eat instead of the rajma and rice?
qa.a: He ate two packets of chips and a fizzy drink.

qa.q: Why did Farhan ask Naveen what he had eaten?
qa.a: He was wondering why he felt heavy and slow while Naveen had so much energy, and suspected food made a difference.

qa.q: What worked well in how Farhan changed his habits?
qa.a: He noticed his own body's signals, compared with a friend and tried a simple swap before the next match.

qa.q: How might Ammi see Farhan asking for a banana?
qa.a: She would probably be pleased and a little amused that he chose it himself without her nagging. 😊

grounding: Shows a child linking his food choices to energy for play.

passage: 'Papa, noodles again tonight?' Mohit looked up from the chopping board. 'Divyansh, we had them yesterday and the day before.' 'They're the best food in the world.' 'They're tasty, I agree. How did you feel at football today?' Divyansh made a face. 'Tired. I sat down after ten minutes.' 'Hmm. Do you know what your body uses for running?' 'Food?' 'Fuel. Noodles alone are like filling a car with half the petrol. Dal, vegetables, curd, eggs, those help you grow and run.' 'Can noodles have vegetables in them?' Mohit laughed. 'Now you're thinking. Sunday special: noodles with peas and carrots. Tonight, khichdi.' Divyansh groaned. 'Okay. But extra ghee.'

qa.q: How long did Divyansh last at football before sitting down?
qa.a: Divyansh sat down after ten minutes, feeling tired.

qa.q: How was Divyansh feeling when asking if noodles could have vegetables?
qa.a: Divyansh seemed curious and hopeful, looking for a way to keep a favourite food while getting more of the fuel a growing body needs.

qa.q: What did Papa do well to help Divyansh think about food?
qa.a: He agreed noodles are tasty and linked food to how Divyansh felt at football, instead of banning them.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had simply said 'No noodles ever'?
qa.a: Divyansh might have felt punished and craved noodles more, without learning why other foods help.

grounding: Shows a parent helping a child connect food choices to energy and growth.

passage:
When I was ten, I ate a packet of chips before every football practice. Salty, crunchy, and gone in a minute.
I'm Ujjwal. By the second half I'd be tired and slow.
Coach Dolma noticed. She asked what I'd eaten. When I told her, she didn't laugh. “Try a banana and a roti with something in it next time. See if your legs feel different.”
So I tried it for a week. Banana and a roti roll with egg.
By Friday I was running as fast in the second half as the first. I still like chips. Now they're for weekends.

qa.q: What did Coach Dolma suggest Ujjwal try?
qa.a: A banana and a roti with something in it.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel by Friday?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt stronger and pleased, running as fast in the second half as the first.

qa.q: Why did changing the snack help Ujjwal?
qa.a: The banana and roti gave longer-lasting energy than chips.

qa.q: How might Coach Dolma feel seeing Ujjwal run faster?
qa.a: She would probably feel pleased that her advice helped.

grounding: A student learns that food choices affect energy for sport.

passage:
Canteen note. Jagdish Singh, school canteen manager.
For most of the term, Baljeet (eleven) bought two samosas and a cold drink every lunch. By sixth period, his class teacher said, he was yawning.
After the health talk last week, I noticed a change. Baljeet stood at the counter, looked at the samosas, then asked for the dal-rice and a banana. He said, “Ma'am said this keeps you going longer.”
On Friday he came back and said he hadn't felt sleepy in maths.
Next step: I've put the fruit near the front of the counter, where children see it first.

qa.q: What did Baljeet usually buy before?
qa.a: Two samosas and a cold drink.

qa.q: How did Baljeet seem to feel after changing his lunch?
qa.a: He seemed pleased and more awake, not sleepy in maths.

qa.q: Why is putting fruit near the front a good next step?
qa.a: It makes healthy choices easier for children to see and pick.

qa.q: How might Baljeet's class teacher feel about the change?
qa.a: The teacher is probably pleased to see him more awake in class.

grounding: A canteen manager notes an eleven-year-old linking food choices to energy.

passage:
Wednesday
Mumma gave me an apple for my tiffin. I wanted the packaged mango juice like my cousin Ujjwal has.
Ujjwal told me his coach said those juices have lots of added sugar and don't fill you up. I didn't believe him.
So today I tried an experiment. Monday: juice at break. I was hungry again by eleven. Today: the apple and some peanuts. I wasn't hungry till lunch.
Ujjwal said, “See?” I said, “Okay, okay.”
I'll still have juice sometimes. But not every day. — Dhruv

qa.q: What did Mumma give Dhruv for the tiffin?
qa.a: An apple.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel about Ujjwal's advice at first, and then?
qa.a: Dhruv felt doubtful at first, then convinced after the experiment.

qa.q: What did Dhruv's experiment show?
qa.a: The apple and peanuts kept Dhruv full longer than the juice.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel after Dhruv's experiment?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably feels pleased, and a bit smug, to be proved right.

grounding: A student tests how food choices affect energy and fullness.

passage:
At the village school, the chips man set up his cart right outside the gate at lunch. Gargi spent her coins on a packet every day and left her roti and sabzi.
By the afternoon kho-kho game, she was always first out. "My legs feel like jelly," she complained.
Arohi, her friend, shared her tiffin. "Try my dal-roti today. Save the chips for Sunday."
Gargi ate it, grumbling. That afternoon, she lasted till the end of the game.
"Must be the dal," Arohi said.
Gargi thought about her empty tiffin. "Or maybe the chips were the problem."

qa.q: Where did the chips man set up his cart?
qa.a: Right outside the gate.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when she said her legs felt like jelly?
qa.a: Gargi felt tired and frustrated at being out first every day.

qa.q: What small step could Gargi try to keep her energy up?
qa.a: Eating her own roti and sabzi at lunch and keeping chips for a treat day, as Arohi suggested.

qa.q: How does Arohi see Gargi's lunches?
qa.a: Arohi thinks the chips aren't giving Gargi enough energy and gently suggests a change.

grounding: A village child notices that eating chips instead of lunch leaves her tired for games.

passage:
At the school in Madrid, Soo-ah traded her lunch for Ines's chocolate bar and a fizzy drink every day for a week.
By the last lesson she was yawning and her head hurt.
On Friday Ines said, "You look sleepy all afternoon."
"I don't know why."
"Maybe the sugar? My mum says it goes up fast, then drops."
Soo-ah thought about her bibimbap, left untouched in her box. The next Monday she ate it. In the afternoon science lesson, she didn't yawn once.
"Just saying," said Ines, eating an apple.

qa.q: What did Soo-ah trade her lunch for?
qa.a: Ines's chocolate bar and a fizzy drink.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling in the afternoons that week?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt tired and unwell, yawning with a headache.

qa.q: What could Soo-ah do to keep her energy in the afternoon?
qa.a: She could eat her own balanced lunch and keep sweets as an occasional treat.

qa.q: How does Ines see the change in Soo-ah?
qa.a: Ines seems pleased and a little smug, having guessed that the sugary lunches were part of the problem.

grounding: A child in Spain links sugary lunches with afternoon tiredness and changes her choice.

passage:
At the sports club canteen, the swimming practice had just ended. Sahil reached for a cola and a packet of fried namkeen.
Harsha, who was in his swim group, took a banana and a bowl of poha.
"That's so boring," said Sahil.
"Coach said we'll need energy for the relay trials tomorrow," Harsha said. "Cola makes me crash."
Sahil looked at his namkeen. He remembered feeling floppy after last week's practice.
He put the cola back and got a banana too. "Fine. But I'm keeping the namkeen."
Harsha grinned. "Deal."

qa.q: What did Harsha take at the canteen?
qa.a: A banana and a bowl of poha.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he looked at his namkeen?
qa.a: Sahil felt unsure, remembering how floppy he felt after last week's practice.

qa.q: What choice did Sahil make, and why is it a good middle path?
qa.a: He swapped the cola for a banana but kept the namkeen, so he improved his snack without feeling forced.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Sahil's switch?
qa.a: Harsha is pleased and doesn't push further, happy with a fair compromise.

grounding: At a sports club canteen, a child links food choices to energy for sport.

passage:
I'm Kashish from next door, and I sometimes watch Parveen's cricket from our gate.
On match days Parveen used to buy two packets of chips from the corner shop and eat them walking to the ground. By the second innings Parveen was always sitting in the shade, fanning with a cap.
Last Saturday was different. Parveen came out with a steel box: a banana, a roti roll and some chana. I heard Parveen's Nani calling after, "Water bottle!" and Parveen ran back for it.
I can't say whether it was the food. But Parveen bowled the whole second innings and was still running when I went in for lunch. Later I heard Parveen tell another kid, "Chips make me sleepy. This keeps me going longer."

qa.q: What was in Parveen's steel box last Saturday?
qa.a: A banana, a roti roll and some chana.

qa.q: What does Parveen's comment to another kid suggest about how Parveen felt?
qa.a: Parveen seemed pleased and proud of noticing that the new food made a difference to playing longer.

qa.q: How could Parveen's Nani keep supporting this choice?
qa.a: Nani could keep helping pack simple, filling food and water on match days and let Parveen notice the difference without lecturing.

qa.q: Why might Kashish be careful not to say it was only the food?
qa.a: Kashish is only watching from the gate, so Kashish can't know everything that changed, like sleep or practice.

grounding: Shows a neighbour observing a child link food choices to energy during games.

passage:
Losar week, and Dolma's house was full of khapse and sweets. Day one, she ate khapse for breakfast, sweets at lunch, more at every visit. By evening she was cranky and flopped on the sofa while her cousins played.
Day three, she noticed. "Why am I so tired? I'm not even sick," she said to Vaibhav, her neighbour, who had come over.
"My mum says sugar goes up fast and down fast," Vaibhav said. "Like a firework."
Day six, Dolma tried something. Thukpa with vegetables for lunch, then khapse as a treat after, not instead. She played with the cousins until dark.
"You're not flopping," her aunt said.
Dolma grinned. "I'm eating like a person, not a sweet box."

qa.q: What did Dolma eat for lunch on day six?
qa.a: Thukpa with vegetables for lunch, then khapse as a treat after.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling on day three when she asked why she was so tired?
qa.a: Dolma felt puzzled and a bit frustrated, because she was tired without being sick.

qa.q: What could Dolma try at the next festival?
qa.a: She could keep having a proper meal first and enjoy sweets as a treat after, so she has energy to play.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see the firework comparison helping Dolma?
qa.a: Vaibhav might feel pleased that a simple idea from home helped a friend notice something for herself.

grounding: Illustrates a child linking festival eating to energy over several days and adjusting her choices.

passage:
Farhan, you ask why I always make you eat sehri, even when you're sleepy. Let me tell you.
When I was eleven, one Ramzan, I thought I was clever. I skipped the dal and roti at sehri and just ate two jalebis, because they were sweet and quick. By afternoon at school I couldn't think. The letters swam. In cricket after, I dropped three easy catches and sat down under the neem tree, too tired even to be angry.
My Ammi didn't shout. She said, "Asif, your body is a lamp. Sugar is paper, it burns fast. Dal is oil." Next day I ate dal and roti. I still felt the fast, but I could think.
So now, beta, eat what burns slowly.

qa.q: What did the young Asif eat at sehri that day?
qa.a: He skipped the dal and roti and just ate two jalebis.

qa.q: How did young Asif feel under the neem tree?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and weak, too tired even to be angry about the dropped catches.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Asif's story, and why?
qa.a: Choosing dal and roti the next day was the turning point, because he noticed he could think even while fasting.

qa.q: How might Asif's Ammi have felt watching him come home tired?
qa.a: She was probably concerned but patient, which is why she explained with the lamp picture instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child he learned that what he ate affected his energy during a fast.

passage:
It was exam week in the December cold, and Tenzin had only forty rupees left for the canteen after buying a pen. The chips and a cola cost exactly that. Dal-rice with a boiled egg cost thirty-five.
His friend Leela was already eating chips. "Treat yourself. Exams are stressful."
Tenzin remembered last week: chips at lunch, and by the maths paper at two he was yawning and couldn't think. Amala had said, "Food is fuel, Tenzin. Some fuel burns out fast."
He bought the dal-rice. It wasn't exciting. But at two o'clock, in the chemistry paper, his head felt clear.
Leela, beside him in the hall, was rubbing her eyes. After, she said, "Maybe dal-rice tomorrow."

qa.q: How much did the dal-rice with a boiled egg cost?
qa.a: Dal-rice with a boiled egg cost thirty-five.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin choose dal-rice even though chips were tempting?
qa.a: He was worried about feeling tired and foggy again in his exam, as he had last week after eating chips.

qa.q: What small step could Tenzin keep doing during exams?
qa.a: He could keep choosing filling meals like dal-rice on exam days and save treats for after, noticing how each choice affects his energy.

qa.q: What might Leela realise after the chemistry paper?
qa.a: Leela might realise her tiredness was linked to the chips, which is why she decides to try dal-rice tomorrow.

grounding: Shows a child connecting food choices to energy during exams, despite a tight budget.
